To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Zn bioavailability assays should be conducted in chicks fed a basal diet from 1 to 21 d of age; 2) Zn bioavailability should be assessed by measuring Zn accumulation in the bone; and 3) Zn bioavailability is not affected by Zn source or by delaying the onset of high-Zn feeding until 7 d of posthatch.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Zn bioavailability assays in chicks are not accurate enough to provide reliable estimates of Zn bioavailability.
the most reliable and accurate bioavailability assays for Zn in chicks are those that use bone Zn as the criterion.
the use of a 3-wk-old chick bioassay is the most accurate method to estimate Zn bioavailability in poultry diets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of Zn sulfate as a source in bioavailability assays is not recommended.
the most reliable and reproducible criterion for bioavailability studies is bone Zn accumulation, and that the most reliable source for Zn in bioavailability studies is Zn sulfate.
the most reliable method for estimating bioavailable Zn for chicks is the use of the bone Zn response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the bioavailability of Zn in feed ingredients is highly variable, and that this is an area that deserves more research.
